mercy_translation.text:
If they do not consider these things sufficient, let them at least be convinced by other sayings which they themselves possess. Of whom do the prophets say: “I became manifest to those who did not seek me; I was found by those who did not ask for me. I said, Behold, I am here, to a nation that did not call upon my name. I stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contradicting people”?

Who, then, is the One who became manifest? Let someone ask the Jews. If it is the prophet, let them say when he was hidden so that he might later become manifest. What prophet is this who both became manifest from being unseen and stretched out his hands upon a cross? None of the righteous did so; only the Word of God, who is incorporeal by nature, appeared in a body for our sake and suffered on our behalf.

If even this is not enough for them, let them at least be put to shame by other passages, seeing so clear a refutation. Scripture says: “Be strong, hands that are weak and knees that are paralyzed. Encourage those who are faint-hearted in mind: be strong, do not fear. Behold, our God repays judgment; he himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear. Then the lame shall leap like a deer, and the tongue of the speechless shall be clear.”

What can they say about this? How can they even dare to face it? The prophecy announces that God will come and makes known the signs and the time of his presence. It says that when the divine presence takes place, the blind will see, the lame will walk, the deaf will hear, and the tongue of those unable to speak will become clear. When, then, did signs like these occur in Israel? Where did anything like this happen in Judea? Let them say.

Naaman the leper was cleansed, but no deaf person heard and no lame person walked. Elijah and Elisha raised a dead person, but no one blind from birth received sight. Raising the dead is indeed a great thing, but it is not the same kind of wonder as the Savior's miracle. And if Scripture did not remain silent about the leper and the widow's dead son, surely if a lame person had walked or a blind person had received sight it would not have failed to report these things. Since Scripture is silent about them, it is clear that they had not happened before.

When, then, did these things happen except when the Word of God himself came in a body? And when did he come except when the lame walked, the speechless spoke clearly, the deaf heard, and those blind from birth received sight? The Jews who witnessed these things at the time said as much, having never heard that such things had happened before: “From the beginning of the age it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

translator_notes: Translated directly from the Greek source.
The chapter reads Isaiah's healing signs as identifying the divine visitation fulfilled in Christ.
Athanasius distinguishes the healing of congenital blindness as a particularly significant sign in his argument.
